questions.q: When the three quarter totals are compared, what is the actual result?
options: All three totals match exactly
Power BI and Tableau match each other exactly; Finance's Excel SUMIFS total comes back slightly higher than both
All three totals are wildly different, off by an order of magnitude
Finance's total is lower than both Power BI and Tableau
questions.explain: Power BI and Tableau agree with each other since both query the same warehouse rows the same way. Excel's SUMIFS total comes back slightly higher.

questions.q: Why is a small discrepancy actually harder to responsibly handle than a large, obviously broken one?
options: Small discrepancies are always caused by currency rounding and can be ignored
A small gap is easy to shrug off as 'rounding' or a 'timing difference' and move on from without actually resolving it — which defeats the point of having an independent check at all
Small discrepancies are impossible to find with any tool
Large discrepancies are always more common in real data
questions.explain: A dramatically wrong number announces itself; a small, real gap is easy to wave away, even though Finance's entire role is to catch exactly this kind of quiet error.

questions.q: What does the fact that Power BI and Tableau match each other, while Excel diverges, already tell you before Chapter 7's investigation even starts?
options: Nothing — all three tools must be checked equally from scratch
It narrows the search to Excel's formula specifically, rather than the shared warehouse — if the warehouse were wrong, Power BI and Tableau would disagree with each other too
It proves the warehouse itself must be corrupted
It means the Python validation script in Chapter 3 must have failed
questions.explain: Since Power BI and Tableau independently query the same warehouse and agree, the warehouse is very unlikely to be the source — pointing instead at Excel's distinct SUMIFS-based mechanism.

questions.q: What does "repeatable" mean in the context of this discrepancy, and why does it matter?
options: The gap can be made to disappear by refreshing the Power BI report
Rerunning all three totals produces the same mismatch every time, which rules out a one-off fluke or a refresh timing accident
It means the gap changes to a different value every time the totals are recalculated
It means only Tableau's number changes on each refresh
questions.explain: A consistent, reproducible gap on every rerun is what confirms this is a real, structural issue rather than a transient glitch.

questions.q: What three independently-built totals are compared in this lesson, and from which lessons do they come?
options: Power BI's CALCULATE+ALL measure (Lesson 12), Tableau's FIXED LOD expression (Lesson 17), and Excel's SUMIFS formula (Lesson 21)
Three different Power BI measures built in three different lessons
Python's row-count check (Lesson 9), Tableau's LOD expression, and a Power BI card visual
The warehouse's raw COUNT(*) check from Lesson 6, repeated three times
questions.explain: Each tool's quarter total was built through a genuinely different mechanism, which is exactly what makes comparing them a meaningful validation.
